title: MODULE 06 — Browser APIs, Asynchronous Programming and Web Integration

overview.text: Modern frontend applications do much more than display HTML and CSS. They communicate with external servers, retrieve information, store user preferences, respond to browser events, handle files, access device capabilities, and update interfaces in real time.
Consider a typical application such as an online learning platform:
A student opens a course, and the frontend retrieves course information from an API.
The student logs in, and the application communicates with an authentication service.
The student completes a lesson, and the frontend sends progress data to the backend.
The application remembers the student's theme and preferences.
A notification appears when a new assignment becomes available.
The dashboard refreshes when new information becomes available.
If the internet connection fails, the application displays an appropriate error instead of breaking.
All these operations involve JavaScript's asynchronous execution model, browser-provided APIs, and communication with external services.
This module develops the knowledge required to implement these features correctly.

By the end of this module, you should understand how JavaScript handles asynchronous operations, how browsers communicate with servers, how to manage external data, and how to use browser capabilities safely.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — JavaScript's Call Stack and Event Loop

blocks.text: JavaScript is commonly described as a single-threaded programming language when discussing its main execution thread.

This means that ordinary JavaScript code executes one operation at a time on the main JavaScript thread. The browser must coordinate JavaScript execution with other activities, including network communication, timers, user interactions, and rendering.
To understand this properly, we need to understand three important components:
These components work together to execute JavaScript applications.
The Call Stack is a data structure used by JavaScript to keep track of which functions are currently executing.
It follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle.
The last function placed on the stack is the first function removed.
function first() { console.log("First function"); } function second() { first(); console.log("Second function"); } function third() { second(); console.log("Third function"); } third();
Execution happens in the following order:
Step 2: third() calls second(), so second() is placed on top of the stack.
Step 3: second() calls first(), so first() is placed above second().
Step 4: first() completes and is removed from the stack.
First function Second function Third function
The important principle is that JavaScript must finish the currently executing synchronous function before continuing with the next operation on the same call stack.
Not every operation is executed directly by the JavaScript engine.
Browsers provide APIs that handle operations such as:
console.log("Application started"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Timer completed"); }, 2000); console.log("Application continues");
Application started Application continues Timer completed
The timer does not block JavaScript for two seconds.
Instead, the browser manages the timer and schedules its callback to run when the required delay has passed and the JavaScript execution environment can process it.
Note that setTimeout specifies a minimum delay, not an exact execution time.
The Event Loop coordinates when queued JavaScript callbacks can execute.
A simplified browser execution model looks like this:
Timers, many DOM events and other tasks
Coordinates queued work when the stack is available
A simplified way to understand the process:
JavaScript executes the current synchronous code.
When the call stack becomes empty, the browser processes pending microtasks.
Once the microtask queue is drained, the browser can process another task.
The browser also gets opportunities to update the screen between appropriate execution cycles.
Tasks, often informally called macrotasks, include:
console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("B"); }, 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log("C"); }); console.log("D");
The timer callback is scheduled as a task.
The Promise callback is scheduled as a microtask.
D executes before the current stack finishes.
The microtask runs before the next task.
This is an essential concept when debugging complex frontend execution.
1.6 Why this matters in real applications
Suppose a dashboard receives thousands of records from an API and tries to process everything synchronously.
Heavy computation can block the main thread, preventing the browser from responding smoothly to user interactions.
Understanding the Event Loop helps developers identify these problems and choose suitable solutions, such as breaking work into smaller tasks or using Web Workers for CPU-intensive computation.
Practical exercise: Write a JavaScript program using nested functions, setTimeout(), and Promises. Predict the execution order before running it in the browser console.
Each operation must complete before the next operation begins.
This execution model is simple and predictable.
However, it becomes problematic when an operation takes a long time.
Consider a function that performs a large calculation:
function calculateSomething() { let total = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 1000000000; i++) { total += i; } return total; } console.log("Starting"); calculateSomething(); console.log("Completed");
The browser cannot execute the following JavaScript on that same thread until the calculation finishes.
During this time, the interface may become unresponsive.
In a frontend application, blocking can cause:
Browser warnings about an unresponsive page
Asynchronous programming allows JavaScript to initiate an operation and continue executing other work while waiting for the operation to complete.
console.log("Request started"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Request completed"); }, 2000); console.log("Other work continues");
The browser schedules the callback while JavaScript continues with other synchronous work.
2.4 Asynchronous does not automatically mean parallel
Asynchronous programming means that execution does not have to wait synchronously for an operation to finish.
It does not mean all JavaScript operations are executing simultaneously on multiple CPU cores.
async function getData() { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); return response.json(); }
While the browser waits for the network response, it can process other work.
However, once JavaScript begins a large CPU-intensive calculation on the main thread, that calculation can still block the interface.
Parallel CPU processing can be achieved with mechanisms such as Web Workers.
Frontend applications commonly use several techniques:
Execute a function after an operation
Write asynchronous code in a sequential style
Respond to actions or state changes
2.6 When to use each execution model
Use synchronous code when operations are short and need immediate results.
Use asynchronous operations when waiting for network responses, browser APIs, file operations, or other operations that complete later.
Use Web Workers when significant CPU-intensive work would otherwise block the main interface.
Practical exercise: Create a page with a button that starts a long synchronous calculation. Observe how the interface behaves, then redesign the operation using a Web Worker.

sections.title: LESSON 03 — Callbacks, Promises and Promise Chaining

blocks.text: A callback is a function passed into another function so that it can be executed later.
function greetUser(name, callback) { console.log("Hello " + name); callback(); } function showMessage() { console.log("Welcome to the application"); } greetUser("Student", showMessage);
Hello Student Welcome to the application
Callbacks are widely used in JavaScript.
function getUserData(callback) { setTimeout(() => { const user = { id: 1, name: "Sam" }; callback(user); }, 1000); } getUserData((user) => { console.log(user); });
The callback executes after the simulated asynchronous operation completes.
This approach was historically common for handling asynchronous tasks.
However, multiple dependent callbacks can create complicated code.
Suppose a frontend application needs to:
With nested callbacks, code can become difficult to maintain.
As dependencies increase, the nesting becomes harder to understand.
This is commonly called Callback Hell.
A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.
A Promise has three possible states:
A Promise settles when it becomes fulfilled or rejected.

const coursePromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const courseLoaded = true; if (courseLoaded) { resolve("Course loaded successfully"); } else { reject("Unable to load course"); } }); coursePromise .then((result) => { console.log(result); }) .catch((error) => { console.error(error); });
Promises allow asynchronous operations to be connected using .then().

fetch("/api/user") .then((response) => { if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Unable to fetch user"); } return response.json(); }) .then((user) => { console.log(user); return fetch(`/api/courses/${user.id}`); }) .then((response) => { if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Unable to fetch courses"); } return response.json(); }) .then((courses) => { console.log(courses); }) .catch((error) => { console.error("Application error:", error); });
Each .then() can return a normal value or another Promise.
If another Promise is returned, the next stage waits for it to settle.
JavaScript provides useful Promise methods for managing multiple asynchronous operations.
Waits until all Promises fulfill. Rejects when one rejects.
const results = await Promise.all([ fetch("/api/users"), fetch("/api/courses"), fetch("/api/assignments") ]);
Useful when all operations are required to display a page.
Waits until all Promises settle, regardless of whether they fulfill or reject.
const results = await Promise.allSettled([ fetch("/api/users"), fetch("/api/courses"), fetch("/api/assignments") ]); console.log(results);
Useful when a dashboard can display some sections even if other requests fail.
Returns the result of the first Promise to settle.
Returns the first successfully fulfilled Promise. It rejects with an AggregateError if all supplied Promises reject.
An educational platform may load several independent resources:
Using Promise utilities can make it easier to load these resources efficiently.
Practical exercise: Create three asynchronous functions representing user, course, and progress retrieval. Connect them using Promise chaining and then rewrite the solution using Promise.all().
async and await provide a cleaner way to work with Promises.
An async function always returns a Promise.
async function getMessage() { return "Welcome to JavaScript"; } getMessage().then((message) => { console.log(message); });
Even though the function returns a normal string, JavaScript wraps the returned value in a fulfilled Promise.
The await keyword allows an async function to pause its own execution until a Promise settles.
async function loadCourse() { const result = await fetch("/api/courses"); console.log(result); } loadCourse();
The async function waits for the network operation, but JavaScript can continue processing other work.
await can normally be used inside async functions. Modern JavaScript also supports top-level await in compatible modules.
Consider a frontend application retrieving course information.

async function getCourses() { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Failed to retrieve courses"); } const courses = await response.json(); return courses; }
Converts the response body into JSON.
Asynchronous operations may fail for many reasons.
We can handle these problems using try/catch.

async function loadCourses() { try { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`HTTP Error: ${response.status}`); } const courses = await response.json(); console.log(courses); } catch (error) { console.error("Unable to load courses:", error); } }
The try section contains operations that may fail.
The catch section handles thrown errors and rejected awaited Promises.
The finally block executes after the try or catch section completes.
It is useful for cleanup operations.

async function loadDashboard() { showLoading(); try { const response = await fetch("/api/dashboard"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Dashboard request failed"); } const data = await response.json(); displayDashboard(data); } catch (error) { showError(error.message); } finally { hideLoading(); } }
Even when the request fails, the loading indicator is removed.
One common performance mistake is waiting for independent operations unnecessarily.
const users = await fetch("/api/users"); const courses = await fetch("/api/courses"); const analytics = await fetch("/api/analytics");
Each request starts after the previous awaited operation has completed.
const [users, courses, analytics] = await Promise.all([ fetch("/api/users"), fetch("/api/courses"), fetch("/api/analytics") ]);
All requests are initiated without waiting for the previous request to finish.
Parallel execution is generally preferable when the operations are independent and every result is required.
Practical exercise: Build an async function that retrieves a user's details and course information. Add error handling, a loading state, and a success message.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — Fetch API and HTTP-Based Data Retrieval

blocks.text: The Fetch API is a browser-provided JavaScript interface for making network requests.
It allows frontend applications to communicate with external servers and backend APIs.
For example, a course platform might request:
JavaScript can retrieve this information and use it to display course cards.
async function getCourses() { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); const courses = await response.json(); console.log(courses); }
The important point is that fetch() returns a Promise.
It does not immediately return the final response data.
The Fetch API returns a Response object.
Indicates whether status is in the 200–299 range

async function getCourses() { const response = await fetch("/api/courses"); console.log(response.status); console.log(response.ok); console.log(response.headers); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Request failed"); } return response.json(); }
A frequent beginner mistake is assuming that HTTP errors automatically reject a Fetch Promise.
For example, a server can respond with:
The Fetch Promise normally fulfills with a Response object.
Therefore, developers must inspect response.ok or response.status.
Fetch rejects for failures such as network errors, invalid request construction in applicable cases, and aborted requests.
The Fetch API supports different HTTP methods.
Create a resource or initiate an operation
const response = await fetch("/api/courses", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Frontend Engineering", level: "Intermediate" }) });
The body property sends data to the server.
JSON.stringify() converts a JavaScript object into JSON text.
The browser can read response data in different formats.
const jsonData = await response.json(); const textData = await response.text(); const blobData = await response.blob(); const arrayBuffer = await response.arrayBuffer();
Choose a method appropriate for the content returned by the server.
A response body is generally consumed once. Do not attempt to read it with multiple body-reading methods unless you deliberately clone the Response first.
An online learning platform might use Fetch for:
Practical exercise: Retrieve a list of courses from an API and display the course titles, levels, and descriptions on a webpage.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — REST API Integration from the Browser

blocks.text: REST stands for Representational State Transfer.
It is an architectural style for designing networked applications.
REST APIs commonly represent application data as resources and use HTTP methods to interact with those resources.
For example, consider a learning platform.
Each resource can have different operations.
An endpoint is a URL through which a client interacts with a particular API resource or operation.
These endpoints allow the frontend to:
Suppose a student completes a lesson.
The frontend might submit the following request:

async function completeLesson(lessonId) { const response = await fetch( `/api/lessons/${lessonId}/complete`, { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ completed: true }) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Unable to update lesson progress"); } return response.json(); }
The frontend communicates with the backend, which validates the operation and updates the database.
A frontend should never assume that a successful button click means the server has successfully saved the information.
A server needs to know which user is making a request.
Depending on the authentication architecture, requests may use:
Do not expose private API keys, server secrets, or privileged credentials in frontend JavaScript.
Anything sent to the browser can potentially be inspected by the user.
Prefer a backend service to handle secret credentials and sensitive operations.
CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.
Browsers enforce a same-origin security policy. When a frontend accesses a different origin, the browser applies CORS rules.
These are different origins because their hostnames differ.
The backend needs appropriate CORS response headers to permit the frontend origin.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://prepspaces.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Some cross-origin requests trigger a preflight request using the HTTP OPTIONS method.
The browser checks whether the server permits the actual request.
CORS is enforced by browsers. It is not a replacement for backend authentication or authorization.
Authentication failure: the user is not properly authenticated.
Authorization failure: the user lacks permission.
Validation failure: submitted data does not satisfy server requirements.
Server failure: the backend could not successfully process the request.
Network failure: the browser could not successfully communicate with the server.
CORS failure: the browser did not allow the cross-origin response to be accessed by the application.
Practical exercise: Build a course management interface that retrieves, creates, updates, and deletes course records through a REST API.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — JSON Processing and Data Transformation

blocks.text: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation.
It is a text-based data format commonly used for exchanging information between frontend and backend applications.
It does not directly represent JavaScript functions, undefined, or symbols.
The JSON.parse() method converts JSON text into a JavaScript value.
const jsonString = '{"name":"Alex","age":22}'; const user = JSON.parse(jsonString); console.log(user.name); console.log(user.age);
Invalid JSON causes JSON.parse() to throw a SyntaxError.
The JSON.stringify() method converts supported JavaScript values into JSON text.
const user = { name: "Alex", age: 22, enrolled: true }; const jsonData = JSON.stringify(user); console.log(jsonData);
This is particularly important when sending application data to a backend.
Data retrieved from APIs is not always in the exact format required by the user interface.
Developers frequently transform information before displaying it.
const courses = [ { id: 1, name: "JavaScript", completed: true }, { id: 2, name: "React", completed: false }, { id: 3, name: "Node.js", completed: true } ];
To calculate the total number of completed courses:
const completedCount = courses.reduce( (total, course) => { return total + (course.completed ? 1 : 0); }, 0 );
These techniques help organize API data for frontend interfaces.
Real-world API responses can contain deeply nested objects and arrays.
Optional chaining can protect against missing intermediate properties:
If an intermediate property is null or undefined, the expression returns undefined instead of throwing an error.
Receiving JSON does not guarantee that its contents are correct.
A frontend should validate important data before relying on it.
function validateUser(user) { return ( typeof user === "object" && user !== null && typeof user.name === "string" && typeof user.age === "number" ); }
For complex applications, schema-validation libraries can provide more comprehensive validation.
Remember that backend validation is still essential. Frontend validation is not a security boundary.
Practical exercise: Retrieve a JSON dataset, filter records, calculate statistics, and display the transformed information in a dashboard.

sections.title: LESSON 08 — Browser Storage: LocalStorage, SessionStorage and IndexedDB

blocks.text: Most frontend applications need to remember certain information between interactions or page reloads.
Browsers provide multiple storage mechanisms for these requirements.
The three important mechanisms in this lesson are:
LocalStorage allows a browser application to store key-value pairs that persist across page reloads and browser sessions for the same origin, subject to browser storage policies.
Remove all LocalStorage values for the current origin:
const student = { name: "Alex", course: "Frontend Engineering" }; localStorage.setItem( "student", JSON.stringify(student) );
Be aware that invalid JSON can cause parsing errors.
However, its lifetime is associated with the page session in a particular browser tab.
SessionStorage is useful for information that should normally be discarded when the tab's page session ends.
Both are synchronous APIs. Reading or writing large amounts of data can block the main thread.
IndexedDB is a browser database for storing larger amounts of structured information.
Unlike LocalStorage and SessionStorage, IndexedDB is designed for asynchronous database operations.

const request = indexedDB.open("LearningPlatformDB", 1); request.onupgradeneeded = (event) => { const database = event.target.result; database.createObjectStore("courses", { keyPath: "id" }); }; request.onsuccess = (event) => { const database = event.target.result; console.log("Database opened", database); }; request.onerror = () => { console.error("Database could not be opened"); };
A real application must also handle transactions, schema upgrades, and database errors.
Browser storage should not be treated as the application's authoritative database.
For example, a student might mark a lesson completed.
The frontend can immediately update its interface, but the backend should verify and persist the student's actual progress.
Browser storage has important security limitations.
JavaScript running on the same origin can access LocalStorage and SessionStorage. This means an XSS vulnerability can expose stored information.
Avoid storing sensitive information, particularly privileged API keys and authentication secrets, in browser storage.
For authentication, a carefully configured server-side session using secure, HttpOnly and appropriate SameSite cookies is often preferable.
Practical exercise: Implement a theme selector using LocalStorage and build an IndexedDB-based feature that saves recently accessed course information.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — WebSockets and Real-Time Interface Updates

blocks.text: 9.1 Understanding the limitation of ordinary HTTP requests
In a typical HTTP request-response interaction:
For many applications, this is sufficient.
However, consider applications that need real-time updates:
Repeatedly requesting information from the server is not always the most efficient approach.
WebSockets provide a persistent, bidirectional communication channel between a browser and a server.
Unlike ordinary request-response communication, both sides can send messages over the established connection.
A student opens an online classroom.
The browser establishes a WebSocket connection to the backend.
When an instructor sends a message, the server can immediately send it to the connected browser.
The frontend does not need to continuously request new messages.
The wss:// scheme provides WebSocket communication over TLS, while ws:// is the non-TLS scheme.
A WebSocket connection produces different events.

socket.addEventListener("open", () => { console.log("Connected to server"); }); socket.addEventListener("message", (event) => { console.log("New message:", event.data); }); socket.addEventListener("error", (error) => { console.error("WebSocket error:", error); }); socket.addEventListener("close", () => { console.log("Connection closed"); });
These event handlers help the frontend respond to communication changes.
Once the connection is open, JavaScript can send messages.
function sendMessage(message) { if (socket.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) { socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "chat-message", message })); } }
The server receives the message and can distribute it to other connected users.
The WebSocket API provides four important connection states:
Frontend applications should check the connection state before sending messages.
Imagine an administrator monitoring a learning platform.
The frontend can process that message and update the activity display without refreshing the whole page.
Real-time communication requires more than opening a WebSocket.
Server-side authorization for every sensitive operation
Heartbeats or application-level connection health checks
For example, the frontend should reconnect when an unexpected network interruption closes the connection, using controlled delays rather than repeatedly reconnecting without limits.
Practical exercise: Build a real-time chat interface with a WebSocket server. Implement connection status, incoming messages, outgoing messages, and reconnection handling.

sections.title: LESSON 10 — File, Clipboard and Notification APIs

blocks.text: Modern browsers provide several APIs that allow frontend applications to interact with files, clipboard contents, and user notifications.
The File API allows JavaScript to access files selected by a user.
For example, a user may upload:

const input = document.getElementById("fileInput"); input.addEventListener("change", (event) => { const file = event.target.files[0]; if (!file) { return; } console.log("File name:", file.name); console.log("File size:", file.size); console.log("File type:", file.type); });
Always validate file types and file sizes on the frontend for user experience, and independently validate them on the backend for security.
The File.text() method can read a file as text.
async function readFile(file) { const content = await file.text(); console.log(content); }
For image previews, object URLs are useful:
const imageURL = URL.createObjectURL(file); const preview = document.querySelector("#preview"); preview.src = imageURL;
Release the object URL when it is no longer needed:
This prevents unnecessary retention of browser resources.
The Clipboard API allows a frontend application to read or write clipboard data, subject to browser permissions and security restrictions.
async function copyText(text) { try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); console.log("Copied successfully"); } catch (error) { console.error("Clipboard access failed", error); } }
A learning platform might use this feature to let students copy code examples or share course links.
Clipboard access generally requires a secure context and may also depend on user activation and permission rules.
The Notification API allows web applications to display notifications through the browser.

async function requestNotificationPermission() { if (!("Notification" in window)) { console.log("Notifications are not supported"); return; } const permission = await Notification.requestPermission(); console.log(permission); }
function showNotification() { if (Notification.permission === "granted") { new Notification("New Assignment", { body: "Your instructor has published a new assignment." }); } }
Applications should request notification permission at a suitable time, normally in response to a meaningful user action.
For persistent notifications that need service-worker integration, the Push API and Service Worker APIs provide additional capabilities.
Practical exercise: Create a document upload component with file validation, an image-preview feature, a copy-link button, and a notification when an assignment has been submitted.
The Geolocation API allows a browser application to request a user's geographical position.
The browser normally requires user permission.
The availability and accuracy of individual measurements depend on the device.
A production application should display meaningful explanations instead of assuming the location request will always succeed.
For applications that need location updates, the browser provides watchPosition().
const watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition( (position) => { console.log( position.coords.latitude, position.coords.longitude ); }, (error) => { console.error(error.message); } );
Stop tracking when it is no longer needed:
This is important for privacy, performance, and resource management.
The MediaDevices API provides access to available media-input devices, subject to permissions and browser restrictions.
const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true });
const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true, audio: true });
The returned MediaStream can be connected to a video element.

<video id="cameraPreview" autoplay playsinline></video>
const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true, audio: true }); const video = document.querySelector("#cameraPreview"); video.srcObject = stream;
The browser receives the camera stream and displays it in the video element.
When a user ends an interview or video call, media tracks should be stopped.
This releases the microphone and camera resources associated with those tracks.
The browser also provides the Screen Capture API.
const screenStream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia({ video: true });
This allows users to select a display, window, or tab to share, depending on browser and operating-system support.
The browser controls the selection and prompts the user for permission.
Geolocation, camera, microphone, and screen-sharing features are sensitive browser capabilities.
Clearly explain why access is needed.
Stop streams when they are no longer required.
Never assume browser permission means the backend may freely use or retain the data.
Most of these capabilities require a secure context, generally HTTPS, apart from specific browser exceptions such as localhost during development.
Practical exercise: Build a video-interview preview page with camera selection, microphone permission handling, screen sharing, connection status, and a button to stop all media tracks.

sections.title: LESSON 12 — Handling Network Failures, Timeouts and Retries

blocks.text: Frontend applications depend on many external systems.
A request can fail even when the code is correct.
A professional frontend application must anticipate these conditions.
Not all errors should be treated in the same way.
Correct error classification helps developers decide whether to retry, refresh authentication, or show a user-facing error.
A request should not be allowed to wait indefinitely when the application has a reasonable timeout requirement.
The browser provides AbortController to cancel a Fetch request.

async function fetchWithTimeout(url, timeout = 5000) { const controller = new AbortController(); const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => { controller.abort(); }, timeout); try { const response = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`HTTP Error: ${response.status}`); } return await response.json(); } finally { clearTimeout(timeoutId); } }
When the timeout expires, the browser aborts the request.
The finally block ensures that the timer is cleaned up after completion.
In production code, it is also important to distinguish a timeout abort from an intentional user cancellation.
A retry mechanism attempts the request again after a delay.
However, blindly retrying every failure can create more problems.
For example, retrying a payment or resource-creation request without an idempotency mechanism may create duplicate operations.
Exponential backoff increases the time between repeated attempts.
A production retry strategy normally adds random jitter to prevent many clients from retrying at exactly the same time.

function wait(ms) { return new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, ms); }); } async function retryRequest(request, maxAttempts = 3) { for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { const response = await request(); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`HTTP Error: ${response.status}`); } return response; } catch (error) { if (attempt === maxAttempts) { throw error; } const delay = Math.min( 1000 * (2 ** (attempt - 1)), 10000 ); await wait(delay); } } }
This is a simplified teaching example. A real implementation should classify errors before retrying and should support cancellation.
Good candidates can include temporary network failures and certain server errors.
Use particular care with HTTP 429 responses and the server's Retry-After header.
Non-idempotent operations without appropriate protection against duplicates
GET requests are generally safe to retry.
PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent HTTP methods, although application implementation still matters.
POST requests may require an idempotency key or another server-side mechanism to prevent duplicate operations.
12.8 Managing frontend loading and error states
A good application should communicate what is happening.
For example, an API-driven dashboard may have these states:
Display a loading indicator or skeleton.
Display a useful message and an appropriate retry action.
Display an empty state instead of a broken interface.
Practical exercise: Build a reusable API request utility with timeout support, error classification, retry handling, and loading-state management.

The interface should remain usable on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
Connect the frontend to one or more external or backend APIs.
GET and POST operations where appropriate.
Do not put private API keys in browser-side source code.
